What Are Activist Investors? signal 1
Charles Schwab · 6:00 · 5,187 views
Read transcript · ~1,292 words · 8 min read

In June of 2024, Elliott Investment&nbsp; Management revealed it had a $1.9&nbsp;&nbsp; billion stake in Southwest Airlines,&nbsp; equal to about 11% of the company. Elliott believed there was opportunity&nbsp; for a turnaround at Southwest, which&nbsp;&nbsp; had seen its stock price cut in half since 2021. Elliott published a plan for changes,&nbsp; including to Southwest's leadership. The hedge fund's stock holdings&nbsp; were large enough to call for a&nbsp;&nbsp; special shareholder meeting to try&nbsp; and bring those changes to life. And in July 2024, Southwest started&nbsp; announcing operational changes,&nbsp;&nbsp; like adding premium seats and new red eye flights.

By October, Southwest and&nbsp; Elliott agreed to a settlement,&nbsp;&nbsp; which included replacing six board&nbsp; members, five of which Elliott handpicked. Elliott's efforts to reshape Southwest Airlines&nbsp; is a form of what's called activist investing.&nbsp;&nbsp; Activist investing can take many forms, but&nbsp; the goal is the same: to influence how a&nbsp;&nbsp; company is run. Activist investors commonly&nbsp; do this by becoming a large shareholder.&nbsp; Often being a large shareholder entitles them to&nbsp; appoint or take seats on the board of directors,&nbsp;&nbsp; which gives them greater access and&nbsp; influence with the company's leadership.&nbsp; Famous activist investors include Carl Icahn,&nbsp; Bill Ackman, Paul Singer of Elliott Investment&nbsp;&nbsp; Management, and so on.

More recently,&nbsp; activist investors making headlines were&nbsp;&nbsp; Ryan Cohen and his influence on GameStop as well&nbsp; as Macellum Capital Management and Kohl's. So,&nbsp;&nbsp; what do activist investors do? And&nbsp; do they add value or extract it? Activists invest in a company if they think&nbsp; they can increase shareholder value by&nbsp;&nbsp; enhancing the company's profitability,&nbsp; efficiency, or structure. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; in the mid-2000s, Daniel Loeb became a major&nbsp; shareholder in Ligand Pharmaceuticals and&nbsp;&nbsp; wrote a famously scathing public letter&nbsp; accusing the CEO of mismanagement.

Loeb&nbsp;&nbsp; joined the board and appointed a new CEO&nbsp; who quickly reduced employee headcount&nbsp;&nbsp; and moved the company headquarters from&nbsp; an expensive San Diego office building. Over the next two years, sales increased&nbsp; dramatically, producing $218 million in&nbsp;&nbsp; cash. By the time Loeb cashed out, he had&nbsp; nearly doubled his $50 million investment.&nbsp;&nbsp; Total revenue for Ligand in 2021 was $277&nbsp; million, and the company had 155 employees.&nbsp; Sometimes activists are less disruptive,&nbsp; like when Carl Icahn's investment fund&nbsp;&nbsp; owned $2 billion of Apple and used his&nbsp; influence to convince Apple CEO Tim Cook&nbsp;&nbsp; to use its excess cash to start a share&nbsp; buyback program to boost the stock price.&nbsp; Another approach activists take is shorting&nbsp; company shares and then revealing an underlying&nbsp;&nbsp; problem that causes the stock to fall so they can&nbsp; profit.

Short-selling activists are often seen as&nbsp;&nbsp; enemies by investors. However, they sometimes act&nbsp; as private investigators and expose malfeasance. For example, electric car company Nikola&nbsp; was touted as a green alternative to&nbsp;&nbsp; fossil-fueled commercial trucks. It raised&nbsp; $12 billion in an initial public offering&nbsp;&nbsp; in June 2020 and exuberant investors&nbsp; helped its market cap eventually reach&nbsp;&nbsp; an intraday peak of $34 billion&nbsp; before even one truck was sold. As suspicion about the company's claims rose,&nbsp; Hindenburg Research took a short position on the&nbsp;&nbsp; company and then issued a report documenting&nbsp; how management had mislead shareholders.

The&nbsp;&nbsp; report prompted an SEC investigation, which&nbsp; resulted in Nikola founder and CEO Trevor&nbsp;&nbsp; Milton being indicted by federal prosecutors,&nbsp; and the company's stock plummeted. Hindenburg&nbsp;&nbsp; never disclosed how much they made on the&nbsp; trade but said it was their largest win.&nbsp; Short sellers aren’t the only&nbsp; activists with a bad reputation.&nbsp; Activists often push for companies to make hard&nbsp; decisions like selling parts of the business,&nbsp;&nbsp; laying off workers, or relocating to&nbsp; areas with lower costs. In the '80s,&nbsp;&nbsp; activists known as corporate raiders would&nbsp; buy up companies and sell off the parts&nbsp;&nbsp; because they were worth more than the whole.

Many activists would argue that companies often&nbsp;&nbsp; become bloated and inefficient, failing to&nbsp; provide value to their customers and risking&nbsp;&nbsp; failure or bankruptcy. They might say that it's&nbsp; better to trim the fat, even if it's painful,&nbsp;&nbsp; rather than let the company die. This leads us to the question of&nbsp;&nbsp; what kind of track record do activists&nbsp; have in adding value to a company?&nbsp; There are a lot of studies around activist&nbsp; investing and its benefits and drawbacks. Many&nbsp;&nbsp; studies have found that activism has provided&nbsp; strategic, operational, and financial solutions&nbsp;&nbsp; in many cases that have led to increased and&nbsp; sustained company valuations.

For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; one influential study found that companies&nbsp; targeted by activist investors saw short-term&nbsp;&nbsp; share price gains of about 7% on average.&nbsp; Another found that activists increased&nbsp;&nbsp; factory productivity and improved&nbsp; company research and development,&nbsp;&nbsp; leading to greater innovation. However, there isn't a consensus on&nbsp;&nbsp; the benefit of activism. While some studies&nbsp; have found long-term benefits to a company,&nbsp;&nbsp; others have found that activists are often too&nbsp; focused on the short term or that shareholder&nbsp;&nbsp; value tends to find the greatest increases if the&nbsp; company is bought out by another company.

Others&nbsp;&nbsp; have expressed concerns that activism gains come&nbsp; at a social cost such as workers being laid off. When it comes to activist investing, the&nbsp; evidence suggests that they tend to add value&nbsp;&nbsp; to individual companies but they're not always a&nbsp; success. If an activist targets a stock you own,&nbsp;&nbsp; research their goals, plans, and time&nbsp; frame before tagging along for the ride.

What is Board of Directors? | From A Business Professor
Business School 101 · 8:38 · 19,438 views

hello everyone welcome to business school 101 have you ever wondered who makes the big decisions in a company like approving a merger hiring a new CEO or determining the company's strategic Direction it all comes down to the board of directors but what exactly is the board of directors who can be its members and how does it work are there some real world examples in this video I will discuss these questions with you section one definition the board of directors is a group of individ ual elected by the shareholders to oversee the activities and decision-making processes of a company they represent the shareholders interests and are responsible for making key decisions that shape the company's future the board of directors plays a critical role in corporate governance ensuring that the company operates ethically responsibly and in alignment with its strategic goals section two members the major members within the board of directors include the following number one chairperson of the board the chairperson leads the board setting meeting agendas facilitating discussions and serving as the primary link between the board and executive management this role ensures that all board members contribute effectively and that decisions align with shareholder interests for example John W Thompson as former chairperson of Microsoft played a key role in the CEO transition from Steve Balmer to satian Adella guiding the board as Microsoft shifted its focus to cloud computing number two executive directors executive directors are board members who also hold key management positions like the CEO or CFO they provide valuable insights from daily operations helping the board make informed decisions that align strategy with execution for example Elon Musk as CEO and executive director of Tesla directly influences the company's strategy particularly in pioneering electric vehicles and renewable energy ensuring Tesla's ambitious goals are operationally feasible number three non-executive directors Neds non-executive directors offer independent oversight bringing external perspectives to the board's strategic discussions without being involved in daily operations they ensure the board's decisions consider a broad range of stakeholder interests for example Cheryl sanberg former COO of meta serves as a non-executive director at Disney providing insights on digital strategy and governance aiding in the expansion of Disney streaming services number four inde dependent directors independent directors are non-executive directors with no material ties to the company ensuring unbiased oversight in areas like audit compensation and governance their independence bolsters the board's credibility and decision-making for example en muli former CEO of Xerox serves as an independent director at Johnson and Johnson offering objective governance and risk management advice which is crucial in navigating complex Global challenges number five lead independent director the lead independent director facilitates communication between the chairperson or CEO and the independent directors ensuring that independent perspectives are effectively represented this role is crucial when the chairperson and CEO roles are combined for example at JP Morgan Chase Lee Raymond as former lead independent director provided essential independent oversight when Jamie Diamond held both the chairperson and CEO roles ensuring balanced board decisions number six committee chairs committee chairs lead specific board committees like audit compensation or nominating overseeing specialized areas and ensuring compliance with their Charter they report findings to the full board and work closely with management for example Robin L Washington as former chair of alphabet's audit committee oversees the company's financial reporting and internal controls maintaining transparency and Regulatory Compliance number seven corporate secretary the corpor corate secretary supports the board by maintaining accurate records advising on governance and ensuring legal and Regulatory Compliance this role is key in facilitating communication between the board and shareholders for example at GE the corporate secretary ensures that the board's governance processes are aligned with regulatory requirements effectively organizing and documenting board meetings number eight observers or advisers non-members observers or advisers attend board meetings to provide specialized expertise or represent specific stakeholder interests though they do not vote their insights help the board make more informed decisions on complex matters for example Mark andreson a venture capitalist served as an adviser at Facebook now meta providing critical guidance during its transitions into new areas like virtual reality and social commerce section three operation the board of directors makes decisions in a company through a structured process here's how it typically Works step one setting the agenda the chairperson of the board often in consultation with the CEO and corporate secretary sets the agenda for board meetings this agenda includes key issues that need to be addressed such as strategic initiatives financial performance risk management and major corporate actions like mergers or Acquisitions step two preparation and distribution of materials before the board meeting materials related to the agenda items such as Financial reports strategic plans and risk assessments are prepared and distributed to all board members this gives directors time to review the information and come prepared for discussions step three board meetings during board meetings the directors discuss and debate the items on the agenda executive directors such as the CEO might present reports on company performance operational updates or strategic proposals non-executive and independent directors provide their perspectives often challenging assumptions and offering alternative viewpoints points to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the issues step four committee input many decisions especially those related to specific areas like auditing compensation or governance are first reviewed by relevant board committees these committees led by committee chairs delve deeper into the details and make recommendations to the full board for example the audit committee might review and approve the company's financial statements before recommending them to the full board for final approval step five deliberation and debate the board engages in deliberation and debate on the issues at hand this discussion is essential for weighing the pros and cons of various options considering the potential risks and aligning with the company's long-term strategy independent directors play a crucial role here by providing unbiased perspectives and ensuring that decisions are not solely driven by executive management step six voting after discussions the board typically reaches a decision through a vote each director has one vote and decisions are usually made by a majority vote in some cases particularly important decisions might require a super majority for example 2third of the votes or even unanimous approval the outcome of the vote determines the board's decision step seven documentation and implementation the corporate secretary documents the decisions made by the board including the rationale behind them and the results of any votes these records are important for accountability and future reference once a decision is made it is communicated to the relevant parties within the What Is the Role of the Board of Directors in Corporate Governance? | Business Law Pros News
Business Law Pros · 2:41 · 384 views
Read transcript · ~464 words · 3 min read

What is the role of the board of directors in corporate governance? In today's fast-paced business world, the role of the board of directors in corporate governance is more important than ever. Recent events have highlighted the need for strong oversight in corporations. Viewers may be curious about how boards influence company decisions and protect shareholder interests. The board of directors plays a central role in corporate governance by overseeing the corporation's strategic direction. They ensure the company operates in the best interest of shareholders. Their responsibilities include setting strategic objectives and approving major business decisions.

This can involve mergers and significant financial transactions. The board also appoints corporate officers to manage daily operations. In addition to strategy, the board ensures compliance with relevant laws and regulations. This compliance helps protect the corporation's legal standing. Just earlier this week, we saw discussions around compliance in light of new regulations affecting various industries. The board rigorously monitors management performance and risk management. They also uphold ethical standards to maintain corporate integrity. This oversight includes reviewing financial performance and ensuring the company meets its legal duties.

Regular meetings are held to maintain transparency. The board documents decisions and keeps detailed minutes of their discussions. The composition of the board is vital for effective governance. A diverse and skilled board supports long-term success. Many boards seek directors with prior board experience and international exposure. This variety of backgrounds helps directors navigate complex decision-making. For instance, having directors with crossindustry knowledge and former chief executive officer backgrounds can be beneficial. These qualifications are essential especially in challenging economic conditions.

Overall, the board of directors serves as the guardian of corporate governance. They guide strategy, oversee management, manage risks, and ensure compliance. Their role is foundational to the corporation's accountability and sustainable performance. As businesses face new challenges, understanding the board's role can help shareholders and stakeholders make informed decisions.
